extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalists and newsroom editors, policy makers, and designers of news/homepage recommendation systems
extracted.subtask_description: Translate Hamilton's economic theory of news into measurable criteria for story selection and homepage placement: model story coverage probability as a function of audience demand, advertiser value, production cost, competition, and externalities. Useful for researchers, editors, and engineers building news-ranking systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHO cares about the story? (Audience size, demographic profile, attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess who cares about the story — the likely audience size, demographic composition, and expected attention (how long/attentive they will engage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories appealing to larger audiences with sustained attention are more likely to be covered. Consider reach (total audience), engagement depth (time/attention), and demographic composition when estimating demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHAT are they willing to pay or do? (Direct payment, ad-attention, sharing behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the audience's willingness to pay or to generate value through actions — e.g., subscriptions, clicks that produce ad-attention, or sharing that increases reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value from audiences includes direct payments and indirect advertiser-attention; include likely sharing/virality and conversion behaviors when evaluating story value.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHO are advertisers trying to reach? (Advertiser demographic targets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how well a story's audience aligns with advertisers' target demographics and the monetizable value of reaching that audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that match high-value advertiser targets receive priority placement even if their total audience is smaller. Measure advertiser-audience match explicitly (e.g., age, income, interests).

rubrics_metrics.name: WHEN does the story have value? (Time-decay of news value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the temporal profile of a story's value — when it is most valuable and how quickly its relevance decays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a time-decay function to score time-sensitive stories; prioritize high immediate value items (breaking news) but also consider longer-lived explanatory pieces for niche audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHERE/HOW is the story produced and delivered? (Production cost, distribution channels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider production and distribution factors: how the story is produced (investigative vs. wire/press-release), associated costs, and available distribution channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower-cost production and easy distribution reduce marginal cost per story, increasing the likelihood of coverage. Factor in channel-specific costs and reach (homepage, mobile, social).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Demand Curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with higher predicted audience demand (appeal to larger or more engaged audiences) are preferred under market-driven selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify demand via historical consumption, predictive models, or proxies (search trends, social signals). Preference is given to stories with sustained, not just fleeting, attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser-Audience Match
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority is given to stories whose audience profile matches valuable advertiser targets; advertiser value can outweigh pure audience size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure demographic alignment and advertisers' willingness-to-pay for those segments. This can cause smaller-but-targeted audiences to be favored over larger but less valuable audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit cost of producing a story influences coverage: high-cost investigative pieces are less likely to be produced than low-cost wire or press-release stories at the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reporter time, travel, legal review, and verification costs. Newsrooms will discount or ration costly stories absent commensurate private returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of Substitutes (competition and differentiation costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When many outlets cover similar topics, the cost-benefit of covering another outlet's story rises; outlets choose niches or differentiation strategies accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate competitive landscape — if competitors already cover a story, marginal value of covering it declines unless a differentiated angle is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Externalities (public-interest vs private value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some stories produce positive social externalities (informed citizenry) but low private advertiser value, leading markets to under-supply them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify public-interest stories that are systematically undervalued by market incentives and note that market mechanisms alone may not produce adequate coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-Size Premium (operational prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction that, all else equal, stories with larger predicted audiences receive favorable placement and coverage probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience-size estimates as an explicit signal in ranking/homepage models; however, combine with demographic value and cost considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic-Match Premium (operational prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction that stories appealing to advertiser-valued demographics are favored even over stories with larger but less monetizable audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ranking, weight demographic alignment with advertiser targets; this can explain prioritization of stories aimed at 18–34 demographics in certain periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-per-Story Discount (operational prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction that low-cost stories (wire copy, press releases, aggregation) are favored at the margin over expensive investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate estimated production cost per story into ranking as a negative factor; cheaper stories will disproportionately populate feeds and homepages absent policy correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution Differentiation (operational prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction that outlets will choose stories that differentiate them from competitors when competition is high and will converge to mainstream when competition is low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model competitive intensity and include a differentiation term: high competition increases incentive to niche; low competition increases convergence to center/major stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Externality-Insensitive Supply (operational prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational prediction that public-interest, low-private-value stories (e.g., complex policy investigations) will be systematically under-supplied by markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag such stories as candidates for subsidies, nonprofit support, or editorial prioritization if the goal is civic information rather than revenue-maximization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative model of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton proposes modeling coverage probability as a quantitative function of demand, advertiser value, production cost, and competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each variable is measurable; combine them (possibly with editorial-judgment variables) in predictive models for homepage ranking. Use measurable proxies and explicitly calibrate weightings to observed coverage patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicts secular trends (soft-news drift, news deserts, audience-segmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the economic framework to explain and predict macro trends: drift toward soft news, formation of news deserts in small markets, and demographic-targeted coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing homepages or policy interventions, consider long-term market forces (cable competition, deregulation, ownership changes) that systematically shift supply; model these forces when forecasting content mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendations affecting production incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton's five policy levers: FOIA/low-cost government information access, expand nonprofit journalism funding, develop norms for hard news, define digital property rights to enable news flow, and subsidize public-interest investigative production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are remedies to realign private incentives with public-interest coverage; include as constraints or levers when designing systems or recommending institutional change to improve supply of civic journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging sociological selection criteria with economic mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use economic variables to operationalize traditional newsworthiness heuristics (e.g., Galtung-Ruge factors) by translating them into demand, cost, and advertiser-value terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting classic journalistic heuristics for algorithmic homepages, map each heuristic to an economic variable (e.g., 'unexpectedness'→attention spike; 'proximity'→audience relevance) so they can be measured and weighted.
